context_blurb:
Ecologists, the scientists who study how living things fit together with one another and with their surroundings, sort nature into levels, like boxes packed inside bigger boxes. One fox, all the foxes of a valley, everything alive in a pond, the whole living planet: each is a different level. Knowing which level you are looking at tells you exactly what to count.

The smallest level is the organism, one single living thing, such as a fox, a maple tree, a mushroom or one bacterium. An ecologist who weighs one red fox every month of a winter and tracks how far it roams is studying an organism.

One step up is the population: all the members of one species living in one area. A species is one kind of living thing, such as the sugar maple. So in a hardwood forest of maples, beeches and birches, every sugar maple growing there, young and old, makes up one population. Maples and beeches together are two populations side by side. A tadpole is a young frog that lives in water and breathes with gills, yet it is the same species as its parents and belongs to their population.

Where one population ends depends on who can meet to breed. Picture two ponds a long way apart, with dry ground between that no bullfrog ever crosses. The frogs of one pond never breed with those of the other, so there are two populations, one in each pond, tadpoles included.

Next comes the community: all the populations of living things in one area, of every kind, from plants and fungi to animals and bacteria. Algae make food from sunlight as plants do, and bacteria, too small to see, crowd the mud at the bottom of a pond; both are as alive as the frogs. So a student who lists only the birds, fish, frogs and insects of a pond has left out its plants, algae and bacteria.

Add the nonliving parts, such as sunlight, water, mud, soil and air, and the community becomes an ecosystem. Follow nitrogen, a nutrient that plants need, around a forest. Tree roots pull it from the soil; it waits in the leaves until they fall; then fungi and bacteria rot the dead leaves and hand it back to the soil. That loop links living things with a nonliving part, the soil, so an ecologist who traces it is studying the ecosystem.

People fit into the levels too. The people of a town are one species, so they are one population, and with the pigeons, dogs, lawns, oaks and soil bacteria they form the town's community. Its roads and houses belong only to its ecosystem. In everyday speech a town's people are its community, but to an ecologist a single species is never a community.

At the top sits the biosphere: all of Earth's ecosystems together, the whole zone where life is found. Microbes, living things too small to see, have been found high in the sky, tens of kilometres above the ground, and small shrimp-like animals live at the bottom of the deepest trench in the sea, almost eleven kilometres under the waves. A biome, such as a desert or a rainforest, is smaller: one great region of similar ecosystems inside the biosphere.

Each step up adds something different. From organism to population you add more members of one species, from community to ecosystem you add the nonliving surroundings, and the biosphere takes in the whole planet. Only the step from population to community adds more kinds of living things, and that step needs no extra land. A single rotting log can shelter a salamander, pill bugs, beetles, ants and fungi in a patch about a ruler's length across, and that tiny crowd is a community. Gray squirrels counted over a whole forest are still one species, one population, so the log's group sits higher, since it holds many species.
